speechtext: If the article which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) has read refers to the extension of the pier or wharf at Quebec, I may say that tenders were advertised for and quite a number were received. speechtext: I would ask the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if he has received any further word with regard to the disaster at Frank. Now that the accredited officials of the government are on the ground, no doubt the government is aware of the actual extent of the disaster, both as to loss of life and loss of property ; and I think it would be satisfactory to every one to have whatever information the government may possess made public.

I may inform my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) that we have received

further information from our officials on the spot, but I am sorry to say that that information is not exact. It is sufficient, however, to show that the damage is of an extensive character. They are proceeding with the excavation, but are not yet able to reporte exactly the damage done. I have two telegrams from Mr. Pearce. One of them is very long, and I need not read it all, as the information it contains is mainly covered by the other. The other telegram is as follows :
Frank, N.W.T., April 30, 1903.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
Smart,
Deputy Minister of the Interior,
Ottawa, Ont.
No Welshmen killed. Reported death of Welshmen incorrect. Canadian-American has all works excepting probably tunnel destroyed. All their machinery installed and new machinery not yet in place, tipple power house, stables with horses, Are houses and all works totally wiped out by rockslide. Whether tunnel 6,000 feet in length will be available for future operations remains to be seen, only damage to other mines being Lille Collieries, French Company, of Grassy Mountain, having one and one-half miles of railway knocked off. Space and site of same covered with rock to average depth of sixty feet.
(Sgd)	WM. PEARCE.
As I have said, it will not be necessary to read the other telegram, which is very long, but I can give some parts of it which may be material.
The following is probably more nearly a correct estimate of loss than any yet : Thirty-four men eight women, twenty children, killed; eleven injured, probably only two or three dangerously, have good attendance. Only two killed in or near mine. Ten dead recovered, remainder nearly all buried under many feet of rock, possibly a few near edge of slide may be recovered. Killed, miners, twenty-one, balance ranchers, merchants, liverymen, engineers, railway contractors, labourers. Six cottages totally destroyed by rock, swept away like feathers and broken into match wood. One partially ruined.
1 en habitations of ranchers and others outside Frank destroyed. All machinery installed and large amount of new machinery near tunnel mouth totally destroyed. Tipple scales, engine-house and all other plant destroyed. Uncertain whether or not tunnel materially injured, probably not.
Is It possible to give a list of those who have been killed ?
I have no doubt it will be forwarded as soon as possible. So far I have received the name of one man only.

House again in Committee on Bill (No. 78) to amend the Militia Pension Act of 1901-The Minister of Militia and Defence.

When the House was in committee recently on this Bill, I endeavoured to explain the object of the Bill, and I discovered that the language of tlie proposed Bill did not correctly express my intentions. The committee rose and reported progress. Since then I have had the Bill redrafted, and it will now read as follows :
Section 3 of the Militia Pension Act, 1901, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :-
7. Time served in the civil service as constituted for the purpose of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, which would be reckoned in computing his period of service for the purposes of that Act, may also be included in the term of service of an officer for the purposes of this Act and in such case the yearly deduction to be made under said subsection 2 of section 5 shall be reduced by the average yearly deduction from his salary as an officer, clerk or employee in the civil service under and for the purposes of the Civil Service Superannuation Act or any amendment thereof.
The Bill simply provides that a civil servant who afterwards becomes an officer of the permanent force, or of the headquarters staff, and who has contributed to the civil service superannuation fund, shall get the benefit of the amount of his contribution if a pension is granted to him as an officer under the Militia Pension Act. That is the object of the Bill, and I believe that it is sufficiently met by the language of the proposed new clause.

This is a general vote for repairs and improvements to harbours and rivers in Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: There was a request made when this item was up before that the hon. minister would furnish us with a list of the harbours owned by the government and those owned by private individuals upon which we are expending public money. Is that list ready yet ?

I have made inquiries two or three times in regard to it and I have just given instructions that further inquiry be made. We have gone into Committee of Supply sooner than I expected we would. I have telephoned over to the deputy to come and to bring among other things the list to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) refers. It ought to be ready to bring down now.

There was another request for the papers in regard to the Grande Vallee pier. I understand the hon. Minister of Public Works was to make inquiries as to whether there were any further statements or further correspondence in the department-first as to who made the application for the expenditure of this money, second as to the deed the government had of the harbour property, or any other papers.

I ordered the most careful inquiry to be made. There seems to have been no petition from the residents of that locality as I am informed by the officials that there is 71
no petition now in the department. Neither have they any record of any petition having been received. Therefore, there are no other papers to bring down. In regard to the deed, as has been stated, the land belonged to Lovell & Co.-I think the name is -and the company entered into an undertaking to give us the right of way over the property. The matter has been referred to the Department of Justice to be put in shape.
There was no deed given at all then; so that what was said about there being a deed was not correct ?
There is an undertaking to furnish the deed which is practically the same thing.
It has not been brought down.

No, it has not been brought down. It was referred to the Department of Justice to be carried out. There was a question as to whether the company had been dissolved or not. It is in the Department of Justice and it is clearly an undertaking to give us the right of way.
Why is it that you will require $5,000 more than you asked last year for these general repairs and improvements ?

I have asked for an increased sum in the various provinces, because I found that for some years past there has been a deficit. There has not been sufficient money for carrying on these needed repairs throughout the country. The country is losing a great deal of money for the sake of a few dollars. Whether from storm or some other reason damage occurs to public works aud there is no money to repair it. This goes on from time to time till the whole work is seriously injured and then it costs many thousands of dollars to repair the work, whereas, if we had had $200 available at the time a great deal of expenditure afterwards would have been saved. I find from the reports of the officials that this is the case almost every year and I thought it would be better to increase the amount by a few thousand dollars, because I believe that in the end it will effect a great saving to the country.
Isle aux Cooidres-repairs to wharf, $1,800.
Where is this and what will the work cost ?

This is in Charlevoix county. This money is required to make repairs to the wharf there which is reported to be in very bad condition. Horses cannot reach it at the present time owing to the condition in which it is.
Wliat did this [DOT]svharf cost, where is Isle aux Coudres, what was the total amount expended and will this finish it ?
The total expenditure was $17,522.
Will this finish it?

The work is finished; this will repair it.
Lake St. John wharf-repairs, &c., $2,500.
What is this for?
This is to provide for improvements and repairs to wharfs and piers on Lake St. John for which there is no special parliamentary appropriation.
It seems an enormous sum for repairs to wharfs on a fresh water lake-$2,500 last year and $2,500 this year.

There are a great many works on that lake. The importance of the district is growing very much and industries are being established there. This appropriation is asked on the report of the local engineer of the department.
Upon what principle do you give money for wharfs on lakes ? Any person might have a wharf on Lake Ontario or Lake Erie just as well as on Lake St. John.

This money is only expended on government works, not upon private wharfs. It is perfectly true, as discussion has shown during this session, that there are a number of wharfs in this country upon which public money has been spent for many years that are really owned by private individuals, or corporations. That does not apply in this case at all. These are works that were built by the Dominion, they are owned by the Dominion and must be maintained by the Dominion.
Why do you erect public wharfs on a small lake like Lake St. John ?

Perhaps I may be allowed to say a word upon this point. These wharfs were begun when I was in office. The Lake St. John district is One of the most important parts of this country now and lam only sorry that more attention has not been given to it in the past. I certainly think that more money should be voted for immigration purposes for that part of the country. It has been neglected in the past by the government. I take this opportunity of ventilating the very large grievance that I tried to have redressed in the past. This government has neglected that part of the country so far as immigra-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
tion is concerned. Now, I want my hon. friends on both sides of the House to understand the question thoroughly. This is one of the most important and one of the most fertile districts in the country. There has been a large immigration promoted by a colonization company which has been working without having help of anybody. They had received about $3,000 a year from this government and that is all. We are building wharfs in Manitoba, and in the maritime provinces to help trade and settlement, and these wharfs are being built for the same purposes in that district. The Lake St. John district is one of the most fertile parts of Canada, and I take this opportunity of urging on parliament the necessity of giving more attention to that part of Quebec, and to other parts of that province also. It is well to settle the west, and I for one am always ready to vote all the money that is legitimately required for the development of the west, but there are other parts of Canada that ought not be neglected.
Hear, hear.

Lake St. John is a very large lake. The government is dredging the mouth of the river to allow settlers to get in, and these wharfs which are around the lake are comparatively small, costing in the neighbourhood of only $1,000 each.

I have here the report of the Colonization Society to which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) refers and I see that they have been greatly helped by the Department of the Interior during the last year. In 1901 they brought in 2,108 settlers, and last year 2,891, an increase of 783 over the previous year. I fully concur In the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that this district should be well looked after by this government.
How many wharfs are there on Lake St. John ?
There are six or seven.

I have been down in that section of the country and I agree with the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) as to the fertile district that is being opened Up, and I would be glad to see done all necessary work for the purpose of developing that section. But when we were on that side of the House we were always asked by the Liberals, on what principle we made expenditures on wharfs in inland waters. We abandoned the principle altogether of building wharfs which were merely local in their utility. We know that from one end of the St. Lawrence to the other, along the great lakes and up as far as Port Arthur, there are some expenditures for harbours, but I am not aware of any expenditures for wharfs. On what principle is the minister going here ?

I do not know any principle except that it is for the general development of trade and commerce. What has been said with regard to this district is perfectly true. Lake St. John is at the head of a very important system of communication by water and railways. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is somewhat mistaken when he says that the Conservative government abandoned this principle, because these very works on Lake St. John were vigorously commenced in 1894 for the development of that part of the country. We are all pleased to know that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) can speak from personal knowledge of the resources of the Lake St. John region. It is not only becoming a first-class agricultural district, but large and important mills are being established there. The principle, so far as I know that would apply to this is, that it affords accommodation for shipping the produce of the farmers and the manufacturers of that district.

Perhaps I could give some explanation as to the principle which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) refers to. If I remember well, the last budget which was submitted to this House by the Tory government, had included in it many items for the ljuilding of these wharfs. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) who was a member of the then government probably knows more about the principle on which these items were based than I do. The principle pursued by the present government is probably the same principle that guided the late Conservative government. I may say that the local government has built a special boat for the navigation of Lake St. .John to help on colonization, but the local government has nothing to do with the building or amelioration of wharfs in these inland waters, and that is probably why the federal government came to the help of the local government in order to contribute its share to the development of colonization in that district. I hope that this explanation will be satisfactory to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart).

Perhaps the Minister of Finance will be able to give us the principle upon which these expenditures are made. I remember that when I was in the government I was hauled over the coals for stating in the House that in a country where we made large expenditures for the building of canals and the Canadian Pacific Railway, particular sections of the country which were only very indirectly benefited by that expenditure required some balancing compensation as it were, from the Dominion treasury, and that small works which might be of importance only to a particular community had a right to a certain amount of consideration. However, I think that the time has passed for that. The Conservative government was of opinion that it had juris-71i
diction over these inland waters, but by the decision of the Privy Council the control over them is now relegated to the different provinces. I think we should now call a halt In the expenditure of large sums of money on works which are of parochial or municipal or at most, of provincial importance. Our expenditures in the future should be on works for the benefit of the Dominion at large. We should confine ourselves solely to expenditures of that class.
No more Tay canals, for instance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: That was a work like the rendering navigable of the Napanee river, both leading to alleged mills, one owned by me, and one owned by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Yes, but I had to pay for the work.
Lake Temiscamingue, improvements, $6,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This is to pay for operating a dredging plant during the season of 1903-4.
Is this to purchase the dredging plant ?
No. The dredge was built by the Depart-inent of Public Works, and this vote is for the maintenance and carrying on of the work.
What amount of work has been done ?
No work has been done. The dredge has just been finished, and we are to put it in operation for the first time this year.
Is this dredge being operated by contract or by day work ?
It is owned by the department, and is being operated by the department.
Does the minister know at what part of the lake *that dredging is going to be done ?

The chief engineer informs, me that he has reported in favour of starting at Vilie Marie on the east side, and working around the public works. The next place of operation will be at the bar or delta formed by the River Blanche at the head of the lake.

Perhaps I may be allowed to say that I made a tour of inspection on Lake Temiscamingue last year. A good deal of attention has been paid to that part of the country, and I had very nearly come to the conclusion that it would be wise to dam the lake. My hon. friend will find, if he follows his wofk with care, as I am sure he will, that although a dredge

will be a useful implement there for small work, it will not answer all the purposes of the improvements that are required. During the fall months the water is very shallow, so shallow that the steamers which ply on the lake are obliged to anchor in the middle of the stream ten or twelve acres from the shore. The dredging which my hon. friend will carry on cannot remedy that state of affairs; no dredging will remedy it. It would not cost a large amount of money to dam the outlet of the lake, and this would afford a uniform depth of water at all seasons of the year. The Lake Temiscamingue district is one of the most important sections of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and by damming the outlet of the lake, the government would serve both provinces. There are very large settlements in both provinces, especially in the province of Ontario. The Blanche river district is being settled in a splendid way. It is one of the finest parts of this country. There are no better colonization lands than those around Lake Temiscamingue. They are very easy to settle and to clear, and the only trouble is that there is no depth of water in the lake iii the fall of the year, when it is necessary to have communication. I hope my hon. friend will kindly take note of my remarks. I have been on the spot myself on two occasions, the last time being last fall. I have given a great deal of attention to the question of the improvements to be carried out there, and I think my hon. friend will find in the department reports which he can use for his guidance. Although the small dredge that has been built will be useful for opening the mouths of the rivers and removing sand bars, it will not answer the purposes we should try to accomplish in view of the large settlements that are going into that part of the country.
What depth of water will you get after the dredging is done ?

Ten feet. I may say that this vote is for carrying out the policy of the department in regard to the dredging. With regard to the work vfhich my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has referred to, I certainly will give it my serious consideration, and look into the reports.
Has there been any report made with regard to the construction of this dam ?

Yes, I understand that there is a report in the department and that the view of the engineer is that this work will be beneficial to the district. I will ask for a report on the cost of the work between now and next session.

Do you not think it would be wiser, if you are going to deepen the water by the construction of a dam, that you should proceed, first with the necessary Hon. Mr. TARTE.
work, which will give a greater depth of water and avoid the necessity of dredging ?

It may be that the best policy would have been to have built the dam first. However, the other policy has been adopted, and even if the dam were built, considerable dredging would be required at places where shipping is done and at the mouths of the rivers. This dredge has been built for that district, and I believe will be of good service.
Is it the intention of the department to build the dam as well as to do the dredging ?
That is the proposition.

I may say that the information which I have had from a friend who was in that district last year is just in accord with what the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works says, that even if you do the dredging, the boats will not be able in the fall of the year to get near the wharfs. There is another question involved in the proposal to dam. What land would be submerged ? I am told that a great deal of valuable land would be submerged that otherwise would be useful for agricultural purposes. That would have to be taken into consideration also.
When I ask for a report on the cost of the work it will be necessary to ascertain what overflowing of that kind it would cause.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what has been the development in that section-its quantity, volume and character ?
I am unable to give any particulars of the trade carried out in that district, but there is a considerable amount of trade done there.
What is the size of the lake ?
Several hundred miles- an interior sea.
Has the vote of last year been expended ?

Yes.
Laprairie-Ice piers and protection walls, $5,000.
This vote is to be applied towards the completing of a section of crib work in connection with the retaining walls built in 1877-8. This is a breakwater and cribwork.
Is the money spent on the report of the engineer of the department ?
Yes.
Is it to lengthen the protection wall built in years gone by ?
It is only for repairs to the present work.
Has there been any accident caused by the ice ?
Yes.
What is the tota' amount expended ?
Something like over $8,000.
Is that to he built in concrete or in what ?

It is intended for repairs to the cribwork.
Mr. POrE. Is that all protection to crib-work ?
It is all cribwork.
Are we to have this expenditure each year ?
It appears so, judging by the experience of a great many years.

I should recommend putting up something stronger, and avoiding that yearly expenditure.
Le Tableau-descente des femmes-Wharf on River Saguenay, $3,000.
This is to complete the work begun by day labour.
Who is in charge of the work now ?
Mr. J. C. Taehe.
Why did you not let it by contract ? I see that the total sum is $8,000.
My predecessor began the work by day labour, and we are continuing it in the same way.

We have often discussed that question in the House. In certain parts of the country I think it is well to carry out the work by day labour. Provided you get good foremen it is all right, but otherwise there is trouble ahead. That work was begun by day labour, and has to be completed in the same way. In Mr. TacliS you have a very careful engineer. Who is in charge of the work now ?
The same man as before.

I hope that the promise of the department will be carried out, and that all expenditure over $5,000 will be let by contract. It may be that in some cases, as the ex-Minister of Public
Works says, it would be more economical to do the work by day labour, but it is not the business of the minister to go against the instructions given by parliament, which are that all work involving an expenditure of over $5,COO should be let by contract.

I said distinctly, when the matter was under discussion, that there were some cases in which it would not be advisable to call for tenders. For instance, when serious damage has been done to a public work it is very difficult to prepare specifications and let the work by tender, and it is better to trust to the judgment of our engineers and foremen as the work goes on. Under other conditions, I am in favour of carrying out the policy of calling for tenders.

When the member representing the district wants to do the fair thing and does not look first to political patronage at any cost, there would not be any great objection to have public works done by day labour, but when he yields to the pressure of unworthy people, which is often the case, and the resident engineer has not the backbone to insist on the right thing being done, it is a dangerous system indeed. After six years of close experience-because I always endeavoured to follow my work closely-I have found that when the member representing the district is an honourable and good business man and does not want to use political patronage, the system of having work done by day labour is not a bad one ; but, of course, on every occasion, the minister must be very careful to stand by the resident engineer if he has confidence in him. If he has not, let him dismiss his engineer.

We had a case brought before us the other evening illustrating what has been said by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). This was a case in British Columbia. You will remember, Mr. Chairman,' that the resident engineer had appointed a person as foreman of a work, a man who had done satisfactory work under him on a previous occasion. But the employment of labourers by the foreman, it seems, was not entirely in accord with the idea of the member for the district. Consequently we find the member writing to the foreman that he would see to it that the foreman had not the opportunity of hiring or discharging men inside twenty-four hours. So he telegraphed to the Minister of Public Works, and the minister speedily dismissed the foreman.

No. If my bon. friend (Mr. Fowler) will allow me, I will explain the : matter as it happened. This foreman had been appointed without permission being i asked of the department. Mr. Keefer, the i resident engineer, had appointed him be* cause, in the previous year, the man had

done good work. I understood from a telegram sent to me that the foreman had not taken the advice of the sitting member so far as the employment of labour was concerned, and the member had complained to the resident engineer. I simply referred the complaint of the member to the resident engineer, who then dismissed the foreman, and appointed another man. That is all. I never gave any order to dismiss that man, but he was dismissed under the circumstances I have explained.

The fact that the man had been employed the previous year and had given satisfaction led the resident engineer to believe that the proper thing was for him to appoint the man again. Evidently, he thought it was not necessary to make these appointments from year to year, and, as a matter of fact I suppose they are not made from year to year. It seems an unfortunate practice and I trust the Minister of Public Works will he guided by the obvious public interest in these matters.

I regret that the new occupant of the position of Minister of Public Works is not willing to give us a better guarantee that, in the future, contracts will be let after tenders publicly called for. He has put in a qualification so large, so elastic, that it can cover any amount of money. In what he stated, he did not even limit himself to items of $5,000 more or less. He, has left himself quite open, if he finds any difficulty in preparing specifications, to spend the money voted by this House by day labour. Now, I have always taken strong ground against the expenditure of public money in this way : and, after having listened to the little story told us by the exminister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) I have not changed my view on the subject. I have not learned a lesson in this committee to-day that would in the slightest degree affect my opinion on the question. I still think that my judgment was absolutely sound, and that public money should be expended by public tender and in no other way. The ex-Minister of Public Works stated that if we could get a member of parliament representing the constituency who would close his eyes to the voters' list, and leave out of consideration any effect that it might have upon him when he sought re-election-in other words, if you could get a man so framed that lie would give up his chance of re-election, that is, a man from whose makeup human nature had been eliminated-it is possible that the system of day labour might be carried out. Still, the hon. gentleman intimated that, even under these circumstances. it would be a difficult task. I think that in view of the lesson thus taught us, the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) might well be more explicit. In the public interest it would be well for him to say frankly that he is determined to spend money only under contract after Hon. Mr. TARTE.
tenders publicly called for. I know, as everybody knows who is doing business, that there may be inconveniences. But I agree with the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that it would be better for us to bear those inconveniences even if they cost us something. It is better for the government of Canada, for the public life of Canada, for the reputation of Canada, and it would be far more satisfactory to the electors of Canada, to pay something if not, in order that we may be sure that the public money is being expended without injury to the public interest, and I know of no way except by public tender. I regret, therefore, that the minister, in entering upon his work as the head of this department, one of the largest spending departments of the government of Canada, has not seen fit to give us a more explicit statement. I trust that the hon. gentleman, for the sake of his reputation, and, I believe, to the great advantage and satisfaction of the country, will reconsider what he stated to us a few moments ago, and will say that he will, in the future, expend all public money by public contract. And I am sure, that, if there are any exceptions to these rules, through some unforeseen catastrophe or anything of that sort, parliament will always be prepared to stand by the minister in taking any special action that the special conditions may demand. But, outside of that, I do not think the hon. minister should assume the responsibility of any latitude whatever beyond the expenditure of public money by contract after tenders publicly called for. Not by letters written to favourites -I do not admit that the government should have any favourites in these matters. We have seen a great deal of that sort of thing since the hon. gentlemen opposite have come into power. We have known of letters written to favourites asking them to tender, and ministers speaking in this House defending such action on their part on the ground that these parties were their political friends, and declaring that when public money was to be expended they were justified in asking for tenders only from their friends. I repudiate that. Let tenders be publicly called for. and let the man who will do the work cheapest and will give the necessary guarantee that he will carry out his contract faithfully-let him and no other receive the contract.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) misunderstood my remark. I made the reservation I did, only so that if there was urgency which, in my judgment and in the judgment of the officers of the department, made it impossible to prepare specifications without sacrificing the public interests, I should be free to take the responsibility of ordering the work done without public tender. But I may explain that since I became Minister of Public Works no work has been done without contract after tenders pub-

licly called for. Of course, It is liard to have a theory or a law that will not work out disadvantageous^ in some cases. If we were obliged to accept the lowest tender in every case, we might be obliged to give contracts to irresponsible people, even at prices for which the officers of the department know the work could not be done. That entails great dissatisfaction and very often loss on the work. However, as long as the law exists as it is to-day, I intend to carry it out to the fullest possible extent.
Hon. Mr. HAGGAIiT. I am glad to hear the statement of the hon. Minister of Public Works, and I am sure he will carry it out.
I understand him to except only cases in which it would require a special Governor General's warrant for the expenditure, that is, cases like the breaking away of a canal bank where it is absolutely necessary that repairs should be done at once. Cases of that kind may occur to justify the government in proceeding at once, and there is provision in the statutes for an Order in Council in such cases. There is a provision that the Governor General may in cases of that kind authorize the expenditure of money. But except cases of that kind, I understand the minister to promise to this House that all expenditures over a certain amount shall be made under contract awarded to the lowest tenderer, if the lowest tenderer is found to be satisfactory and can perform the work.

There are cases where damages have occurred and specifications could not be made up until a part of the work had been torn off, which often uses up a good part of the expenditure. But, practically, I think the hon. gentlemaju agrees with me on the class of work.

I do not know what the Auditor General thinks now. But, when I left office he had made up his mind that every piece of work would have to be let out by contract, because he claimed that he had legal advice on the point, and that the Order in Council, which was adopted ten or twelve years ago making it obligatory to call for tenders for works costing over So,000, was illegal, ultra vires, and he declined to abide by it. In point of fact, when I left office there were several works required for which he had declined to pay because he was under that impression. I would like to know how the matter stands at present. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Finance might tell me how the Auditor General views that question now.
I think the Auditor General is behaving very well.
I would like to know if the Auditor General is standing by his guns, or if he has becpme milder.

During the short time I have been in office I have not done, apparently, anything wrong, because he has not censured me yet. Perhaps after I have had more experience,
I may do something contrary to law, and he will call me down.

That is not a clear answer. I would like to know from the hon. Minister of Finance, who follows these things closely, whether the Auditor General is still of the opinion that all work for which money has been voted has to be done by contract.

I did not understand the hon. gentleman's question. The Auditor General did take that position and still holds it, and I believe he is endorsed by the opinion of the Department of Justice. It may be a question whether the House should be asked to pass legislation in regard to that matter before the session is over.
Then he wants every work, whatever it may cost, to be tendered for ?
Yes.
He was within the law. The law had been violated for twenty years, and he determined to abide by it.
Oh, well, the violation of the law has not been as bad as they say.

I am glad to hear from the hon. Minister of Public Works a confirmation of my opinion as to what the law was. Some time ago I thought that the hon. Minister of Justice held a contrary view, but I am glad to hear now that he agrees with the Auditor General that all works for which the parliament of Canada lias voted a sum of money must be done by tender and contract, after open competition. I am sorry to hear from the Minister of Public Works and from the Minister of Justice that there is any intention of bringing in a Bill for the purpose of amending the law on that subject.

My hon. friend does not understand the point. He himself has stated, even during the present session, that he thought the department ought to have power to expend the money without tender where the sums were less than $5,000.

Oh, that is the Order in Council ; but the Act is strict in reference to the matter, that all sums of money which are voted by parliament for the purpose of doing any particular work must be expended by contract.

I The hon. gentleman would not say that a

case in which the public interest required it, the department should not have the power to do what has been done for many years under that Order in Council, and to spend small sums of less than $5,000 at the discretion of the minister. I think that was the change X suggested. If the Auditor General, backed up by the Justice Department and by the action of my hon. friend when he was in the government, thought that the expenditure was ultra vires and that a former government were acting illegally, as well as the present government, then I say that it is better we should understand where we are, and if it is in the public interest, that we should ask for an amendment of the law. That is what I referred to.
Hon. Mr. ROSS, (Victoria, N.S.). I think the rule should be invariable that all new works for whatever amount should be let by tender and contract. That has been my own rule in every case, and it relieves members of parliament from being troubled. People come to them and say :	You give
this man work and he voted against you at the last election, and a lot of stuff like that. If you let out the work by tender and contract invariably, you relieve yourself from all trouble of that kind. But there are cases like repairing an old wharf where you do not know when you commence, what amount of work will actually require to be done. You may find that the covering is gone, and some of the logs have gone, and you find that you will require to expend a larger amount than you at first supposed. There are some exceptional cases of that kind where it is absolutely necessary to have the work done by day labour.

During my term of office, if I have not seen fifty members of parliament who have come to me and asked me not to award the contract to the lowest tenderer because he was a political opponent, I have not seen one. Now, I may just as well let out the truth. It is not a question of party, but it is a fact that members of parliament do not like to see public works going to their opponents, even when they are the lowest tenderers. On many occasions I have seen men who were thoroughly honest, but who were members of parliament-
Human nature.

Human nature, as my hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Pope) says, and he knows all about it. Of course, the lowest tender system is the only feasible one when you ask for public tenders. If you get away from that beaten road you do not know where you are at all. Human nature comes even into that.

In asking for the lowest tender the guarantee of the man is a sufficient safeguard that he is a bona fide tenderer. I agree with the ex-Minister of Pub-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
lie Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and I rose to say that I am very much pleased to hear from the hon. Minister of Public Works that it is his intention, so far as it is possible, to carry out the law, and also to know that it is not his intention to have the law amended to such an extent
Oh, oh.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) should not laugh.
I beg your pardon.

I will not do it again, but I have these serious moments in my life, and this is one of them. When I relapse into one of them I am entitled to respect and a sad reception, and I should not be laughed at. I askj for your protectin, Mr. Chairman.

Am I right in understanding that the hon. Minister of Public Works has said that the Auditor General would allow no expenditure on public works, either repairs or original work, unless the work is let by contract ?
Or purchase of any kind.
That is the law.
I believe he says that is the law.

It is a very inconvenient law in my judgment, because there are many repairs in regard to which it would be a saving to the country if they were made by day work. I know that when you have to advertise for tenders for small repairs, there will be more money spent in advertising than would do the whole work. There is a great deal of delay as well.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) express that opinion. That is the position I have taken. It seems to be ridiculous and absurd to say that where a public work has been damaged to the extent of $30 or $300, and when the department has an appropriation for the purpose of repairing the damage, it cannot prevent much greater damage by spending that money under the direction of one of its engineers or other official of the department. It is held now that under the law this cannot be done. A break might occur in a public work, and perhaps two pounds of nails, if properly driven by a man, would preserve the work from great damage resulting. The Auditor General would not pay for the nails or for the day's labour required to do the work. The thing is absurd and after consideration as to what would be the best amendment to make, I have referred the question to the Department of Justice for an opinion, because this interpretation makes the department unwork-

able. It is ridiculous to say that the department cannot make an expenditure for $20 or $30 worth of work without advertising ih five or ten newspapers, costing far more than the work itself. There must be some limitation to this provision of the law. Generally speaking, I agree with my hon. friend, no matter what the defects may be, that the only way we know of is to advertise and let the work by public tender.
What amendment do you propose to make to the Act ?

I have referred the matter to the Department of Justice, and I have asked them to consider it. If that is the law, we will have to have some amendment to it. I should say that an amendment on the lines the hon. gentleman spoke of would be quite sufficient ; that is, that this provision of the law should not apply to works costing less than $5,000.
L'tle d'Alma-removal of rooks, $1,500.
What is this for ?
This is for the removal of rocks at the discharge of Lake St. John, to prevent overflowing.
Where is L'lle d'Alma 1
It is at the discharge of Lake St. John.
Has it been fully decided to blast these rocks ?
The engineer informs me that it has been decided to continue this work. The work has already been commenced.
What is the cost of it ?

This will complete the work now proposed.
Lower St. Lawrence, removal of rocks, &c., $3,000.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC !tKS. This is for the removal of rocks and obstructions in different places along the St. Lawrence. Reports are coming in continually, so I am informed by the officers of the department, of the existence of rocks in harbours and other places.
Where do these rocks come from ?
I do not know ; they are brought down by the ice probably.
Where is it that you intend to make the expenditure ?
In the various harbours along the River St. Lawrence, not at any particular place.
This amount appears to be voted every year. Is it to be continued every year ? Is there any way of stopping it ?
I believe the experience of the engineer to be that this is a necessary vote from year to year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is the money expended every year ?
In some years it is not fully expended. Last year there was only $422 expended up to the 31st of December.
Where is the rest of the money ?
It is perfectly safe in the treasury of the country, and will not be expended unless it is necessary.
You expended $3,000 last year.
I was speaking of the current year. I spoke of the expenditure up to the 31st December last. There was only $2,082 spent last year.

I really think the country can do very well without that vote. Of course, it is in the estimates, and I suppose it will have to go, but the department will be a great deal better off without it. During the last year or two I was very reluctant to put it in again. This is a vote that does not do much good.
They will do something to earn the money.

I do not say that it would not be useful at times to remove rocks fof the fishermen, but we should not remove anything else but rocks. I would impress upon the hon. minister the necessity of supervising carefully the employment of that money. I had a good deal of trouble myself, and I think it is .iust as well that I should help the hon. gentleman with my experience. Let him give strict instructions to his resident engineer, and by the way, who is the resident engineer now in that part of the country ?
Mr. Bertrand.
Do I understand that the engineer has been removed from his position ?	[DOT]
No. There was so much work going on in that district that Mr. Bertrand was put specially in charge, but Mr. Breen has not been removed.
\ Where is Mr. Breen located ?

He has always been located at Quebec.

lion. Mr. TARTE. What district has he in charge at present ?
The chief engineer tells me, the counties of Portneuf, Levis, Quebec and LotbiniSre.
Has Mr. Bertrand's salary been increased ?
No.
I do not ask the question because I make any complaint, but simply for information; he is a good employee.

I thought the works on the lower St. Lawrence and the expenditure in connection with them, had been transferred to the gentleman who came from Montreal to take the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries. Under what system is this money expended now ?
There has been no change that I know of. The money is expended under the supervision of the chief engineer.

Am I to understand that the crop of recks is increasing to such an extent that it is necessary to have a special engineer to take care of them. If we pav this extra man $1,800 a year out of the $3,000 voted, it will be one way of getting rid of the money that is supposed to be devoted to the rocks.

My hon. friend is labouring under a little delusion. This is one of his serious days and we know that when he gets serious he sometimes labours under delusions. There is no new engineer appointed and no change in the organization whatever. As to the crop of rocks they seem to continue about the same from year to year, and have foT a great many years past. Obstructions form and these require to be removed, and it is only a very small incident in the work of the resident engineer to oversee the expenditure of that money.
The minister says that the expenditure was only $2,000 last year. It would appear from the estimates that the whole $3,000 has been expended.
The Auditor General's Report shows that the expenditure of last year was $2,093.22; the balance lapsed:

Then the department intends to expend the money up to the 30th of June next. There was a vote of $3,000 last year, no revote is asked for, and the minister intends to spend that $3,000 up to the 30th of June next. This $3,000 is for next year.
Yes.

This item of $3,000 has been in the estimates since confederation, and has been voted each year. Some years the amount is not spent at all, and I would be much surprised if the Auditor General's Report would show that more than five or six hundred dollars was spent last year out of this item. This money is usually spent in the counties of Rimouski, Bo'naventure, and Gasp6. The object of the vote is to remove obstructions which form in these small harbours which are utilized by the fishermen. It is a very useful vote indeed for the fishermen, because this part of the coast has no protection whatever and wheu the entrances to the rivers or creeks are blocked these obstructions are removed at a small expenditure of $100 or $200. This vote has always been spent with a great deal of caution during the last few years. I have myself refused to recommend the spending of any part of this amount whenever it was not really required.
This is an item that may very well engage the attention of the minister, because the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) suggests that it should be struck out of the estimates.
Not quite.
We have the further explanation from the hon. gentleman from Gasp 6 (Mr. Lemieux) that he himself has refused to recommend the expenditure of this money.
When it was not necessary.

Perhaps I misunderstood the hon. gentleman. I understood him to say that he had refused to recommend the expenditure of money. It looks as if these items were given for the support of the representatives of the people in the different counties along there.
No, no.
I am just taking my hon. friend's own words.
You misunderstood me.
Then what did the hon. gentleman say ?

I said that I myself had refused to recommend to the minister the spending of any money out of this vote when it was not required. I say that for a few years the money has been spent in a straightforward and honest way. It would be a sad thing indeed if the fishermen along the coasts of Rimouski, Gasp6 and Bonaven-ture were deprived of the opportunity, when the entrances to their harbours were obstructed, of having some of this money used to remove the obstructions. This is the only money that could be used for that purpose.

On many occasions, as my hon. friend knows very well, most

preposterous applications have been made to the department for the expenditure of this money. Unless the resident engineer receives most positive orders to spend the money only for the removal of rocks, there will be trouble in the future, as there has been in the past. On one occasion especially money was spent in an improper manner without my knowledge, and from that point of view this is a dangerous item. But if the resident engineer is a firm man, and does not allow money to be spent right and left without reason, it will be all right. I know that my hon. friend is right when he points out that sometimes, after a storm, for instance, a small fishing harbour may be closed. In such a case some of this money should be immediately used to remove the obstruction. But I had so much trouble and misery about this item that I had nearly made up my mind not to apply for it again. But if my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works gives his attention to the expenditure of that money, I am sure it will be spent properly. All the officers of the department who are cognizant of the facts will tell my hon. friend that he has to be careful, because people in that part of the country do not always understand what the removal of rocks means. They may understand it to mean the building of a road or something of that kind, and they will apply for the expenditure of some of this money for the purpose. May I ask if Mr. Bertrand is the only engineer for that district, or has he an assistant under him ?
No, he is the only engineer.
Has he charge of the Magdalen Islands as well ?
No.

The remarks of the exMinister of Public Works bear out what I have said. All the representatives may not be as honourable as the hon. member for Gaspe in regard to items of this kind. If we have a resident engineer, he should perform his duties, irrespective of any recommendation made by any representative or by any defeated candidate. The Conservative party, when in power, no doubt had the same experience to some extent; but I know from my own personal knowledge that they refused to be guided by representatives supporting the government and relied on the officers of the department. I think no representative should have anything to say about the expenditure under an item of this kind, but it should be left solely to the officers of the department.

I would suggest, for the safety of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, that no money be spent without the sanction of the chief engineer of the department. That is the only safe way of doing the right thing. I know the pressure that is brought to bear on the resident engineer, and my hon. friend from Gaspfi will share my views, I am sure.

I may say, in answer to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) that I do not claim to be more honest than himself or any other member of this House; but I say that in the past as at present the representatives of the people have been obliged to correspond with their electors. I receive many more letters about the county of Gaspe, and my hon. friend receives many more letters about his county, than the department or the officials of the department receive; and the member is obliged to go to the department and make the demand or present the petition. In this particular case several petitions were sent to me during the last five or six years, and I could not take it upon myself to order the expenditure of the money. I appealed sometimes to Mr. Breen, who was the resident engineer, that is to -say, on paper, because his residence was in the city of Quebec; but invariably Mr. Breen received his orders from the Minister of Public Works, or during the ministers absence, from the acting chief engineer, Mr. Lafleur; and I repeat again, never in my life would I think of myself giving permission to any of my constituents to spend the people's money without an order of the Department of Public Works. Really, I know more than that.

If the resident engineer wanted to perform work there, and the hon. gentleman took it into his head to say, * no, you will not do it,' would he be Justified ? If the engineer's attention had been drawn to some rocks in the river, and he felt disposed to remove them, surely the hon. gentleman would not undertake to say that he should not do it.

I thank the hon. gentleman for his lesson; but surely he does not think that I would take such a position. When the resident engineer recommends a certain work, what have I to say ? He has no orders to receive from me. He receives his orders from the department. But, I repeat again, the member of parliament sometimes receives letters or petitions from his constituents, and he is obliged to communicate them to the department. That is liow the member of parliament comes in.

I believe the member of parliament is doing his duty then, but when he does that his duty ceases. The moment he steps beyond that and interferes with the officer of the department, he goes beyond his right.

Who says that the member of parliament interferes with the resident engineer ? From what does the hon. gentleman infer that ? Does he find interference in the county of Gaspf or anywhere else ? I think my hon. friend is at sea.
The bon. gentleman made the statement In this House that he had refused to recommend certain expenditures.
Yes, which were asked by some people, but which were not recommended because they were not wanted.
By what right or authority does the hon. gentleman take upon himself- to refuse to recommend any expenditures ?
I received information from interested parties and it happens sometimes, as the hon. member for Compton says, that expenditures are requested which should not be made.

What I wish to point out is that when an hon. member receives such communications he should turn them over to the department and have the departmental officer investigate and make his recommendation, and the department would be held responsible. Otherwise the department may be misled by representatives supporting the government. Misrepresentations of that kind have been made to departments before, and votes have been passed which if, the minister fully understood the details, he would never have allowed to pass.
Perhaps the hon. minister will tell the committee in what counties the money was spent last year and under whose recommendation.

The money is only expended on the report of the departmental engineer. There is no law or custom against any hon. member of this House, either Liberal or Conservative or any other citizen, making representations to the department, as to what work they consider should be done, but the money is only expended on the report of the resident engineer, approved by the chief engineer of the department. If it should be found that any resident engineer has reported iu favour of an expenditure which should not be made, then the only thing the minister can do is to dismiss him. There has been only expended some $400 during the present year, which shows that the resident engineer only recommended expenditures which are in the public interest.

I would invite my hon. friend to call for the records for the past year on this expenditure before spending any more money. These will teach him to be careful. I must say that the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) never recommended to me, when I was Minister of Public Works anything wrong, but there has been a good deal of trouble connected with the expenditure and there will be more in the future, unless great care is exercised. The riding is a very large one and its representatives cannot possibly know all the details and may just as| well be imposed upon ns any one residing 300 or 400 miles from the rid-
ing. The only safe way of spending public money is to have an examination by the resident engineer and have his report sent here to Ottawa.
We will do that.
This debate has brought out the fact that there is a misappropriation of public moneys.
That there was.
And it is now being continued. According to the hon. member representing that riding, a portion of this money is used for the purpose of opening up small streams.
No, to remove obstruction.
In these streams, but not in the St. Lawrence.
Flowing into the St. Lawrence.

Yes, but not the St. Lawrence, and this is an appropriation for removing rocks from the lower St. Lawrence. Therefore there has been an improper expenditure. Certainly the explanation given by the ex-Sfinister of Public Works and the member of the county is to the effect that applications at least have been made for improper expenditure, and there is a good deal in the suggestion of the Minister of Public Works that the item should be struck out. It may be said that there has not been any improper expenditure, but the fact that there have been applications for such expenditure and that they were "refused, would imply that there have been improper expenditures from time to time, and it would be better not to vote the money.
Magdalen Islands-breakwater and piers,
$20,000. [DOT]
There are four different places where this money is to be expended.
The hon. gentleman cannot expect to complete the works at these places with the money he is asking. Does he propose to ask another vote in the sup-plementaries ?
My chief engineer says that this is the full amount that can be expended on those works during this year.
How much will be the expenditure at each place?
At Grindstone the estimate is a little over $8,000. At Pointe a Elie, $4,000, and at Grande Entr6e a little less than $1,000.
What is the length of the work which is being built at Grindstone ?
Is the work nearly completed ?
The chief engineer thinks that the appropriation out of this will complete the work.
Altogether 365 feet.
What is the object of the work ?
This is for piers at the various places.
Are they to be built at towns or ports of any size ?
The population of the Magdalen Islands is about 6,500. Before 1896, there was no wharf, pier or breakwater.
Were there any people before that time.

Yes, a great many. The late government had spent about $80,000 for a pier at a place called Etang du Nord, but it was carried away in a storm. The various works that h%ve been made within the last few years have been very useful to navigators and fishermen. The Magdalen Islands, as you are aware, Mr. Chairman, are the first land passed by the vessels coming from Europe. Those vessels will now find here ample protection from storms.
Is the Etang du Nord work altogether gone ?
The engineer informs me that it is completely gone.
Are the people scattered over the islands, or do they live at one centre ?

There are five islauds, all inhabited.
Maria-Pier, $21,000.
This work is under contract, and the present vote is to complete it.
How much has it cost ?
The contract is for $24,700. The total cost is estimated at $26,000.
Where is this work ?
In Bonaventure county.
Is this a very large place ? Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure). According to the last census the population of the parish of Maria is 2,460. It is the second largest parish in the county.
Is there any other pier accommodation ?
None whatever.
Is this the first they have had ?
Yes.
How have they got along hitherto ?

They ran the risk of losing their lives and their goods landing on the open coast, as they do generally on the Gaspd coast. They are a hardy race of people, as the hon. gentleman knows. Still, lives are often lost. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) would visit Gasp6 and Bonaventure, not only during the fine season of the summer, but early in the spring or late in the fall, he would see the great disadvantages these people have to overcome and the dangers they have to face.
I would rather go in the middle of summer.
Does the hon. minister intend to continue the work to the shore or will he leave this as it is, an isolated block ?
There is an application before us to continue the work to the shore. But there is not enough money in this vote for that purpose.
Has the minister a report as to the cost of the extension to the shore ?
No.
How far would the extension be of this pier or block ?

About one thousand feet.
Murray Bay-Increasing height of wharf and extending same, $4,000.
This is a revote of the appropriation of last year, and is to make provision for the carrying out of projected improvements on the upper south-west side of the west block of the Murray Bay wharf.
Was any work done last fall on this wharf ?
No.
Is this work owned by the government ?
Yes.
Why was not the money expended last year ?
The work is now being commenced, and probably, about half this amount has been spent.
There must have been some urgency for this work last year, the money having been voted. Why were not the repairs made then ?

As I know the place, perhaps the hon. minister will allow me to say that the reason why the money was not expended probably is that when the House rose after last session the passenger traffic was on and it would have interfered with the passenger traffic to carry out the work then. As my hon. friend (Mr. Pope) knows this is a summer resort, and the passenger traffic is heavy.
What was the amount of wharfage received last season 1
That is in control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) is present, and perhaps he can tell us.
I understand the hon. Minister of Mariae and Fisheries has not the returns here. We can furnish the particulars if the hon. members desire it.
It seems to me that this should be brought down. With the minister and the ex-minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries present, we ought to be able to get this information.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) will refer to the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, he will find the returns of this and other similar works, and these figures will be more reliable than any given from memory by the minister.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries acts in a sort of double capacity, according to the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister. He is a sort of deputy assistant Minister of Public Works, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned. Therefore, I think, we are justified m asking this information from him, and it should be given us before the vote Is passed, so that we may judge whether this appropriation for the Murray Bay wharf is a commendable one.

My j?on- friend (Mr. Fowler) will excuse me . * *-p!1 him that that information was furnished him before the estimates were brought down. It is rather unreasonable to complain of information not being given when the information was placed in his hands before the vote was asked for.

But the minister is supposed to be there to answer questions We have not the public accounts before us.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine.) According Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
to the Auditor General's Report the receipts for 1901-2 were $163.69. Further details are to be found in the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Can the hon. minister tell us what the receipts were the year before, so that we may be able to strike an average ?

I doubt very much whether the amount now asked for is sufficient. Of course, the chief engineer must have looked into the matter. But I would call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to the importance of equipping this harbour well. There are several thousand tourists summering there, many of them Americans, and some of them are from Toronto and the province of Ontario. It is becoming quite a large town, and it is important to encourage that summer trade. I would advise him to keep the harbour in good shape so as to give accommodation to the large travelling public who summer there.	*

As the minister was not able to inform the committee how much the earnings were for a year, I may say that according to the Auditor General's Report they were $217. That was a considerable falling off from the previous year. I would like to have an explanation of that.
There was a loss of traffic, I suppose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Since we are on the question of docks, may I ask what amount is derived from the government docks at Midland, Ontario, and the storehouses thereon, and how many applications, if any, have been made for the use of the buildings ?
If the hon. gentleman will wait until I come to my estimates, I will give him all the information I can. I am not in a position to give it now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I notice that a sum of $6,000 was voted last year for Murray Bay, and one hon. gentleman suggested that some of this money was spent in connection with the Richelieu Navigation Company. Would the hon. gentleman say whether this property belongs to the government ?

The government own the property. The province of Quebec owned it before confederation, and it cost them $50,000 or $60,000. Since confederation $40,000 or $50,000 more have been spent on it. It is a very important point, and is owned by the Dominion. So far as I know, none of this money has been expended for the benefit of the Richelieu Navigation Company. Of course, their I boats stop there daily and use the property, j Otherwise, I do not think that there is any-| thing irregular in the expenditure of this

amount. It is simply to complete the improvements and repairs that are going on.

I may add that this county is deprived of railway communication, and this is the only means of communication they have in summer. The Richelieu Company, which is controlled by the friend of my hon. friends, give, I may say, a very good service, which is a credit to the St. Lawrence river. I may also add that Murray Bay is the great summer resort of the lower St. Lawrence, and is mostly inhabited during the summer by some of our good people from Ontario.

I notice that the item for this purpose last year was $0,000. Evidently $2,000 of that has been spent, or will be, at the end of the current year, because $4,000 of this is a revote. The item says :
' Increasing the height of the wharf and extending the same.' What kind of work have you going on there that only requires an expenditure of $2,000 ?

It is an extension of the wareroom, and provides for increased accommodation for handling! the freight. There has been a great increase of passenger traffic at Murray Bay, and there is a great deal of baggage, as well as the freight that comes for other people.

The Deputy Minister of Public Works reports that the traffic at Murray Bay is falling off, hence there is a loss of revenue, not only in the last year, but the year before. Now, the Minister of Public Works states that the reason why this money is required is for the purpose of extending facilities for the increase in the traffic. How does the department settle this question ?
The traffic might increase without affecting the revenues of the Marine department.
It certainly should not fall off.

It is not fair to say there is any inconsistency. Every member knows that there have been great improvements, and since that splendid hotel was built, which is a credit to Canada, a large number of tourists go there, and the passenger trade has considerably increased.

When the ex-Minister of Public Works left that department and the present minister assumed the position it was reported throughout this country that the department was divided, and that a portion of the duties were transferred to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Would the hon. gentleman tell us what portion of the duties of the Public Works department is under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, so that we may know to whom we should address our questions ?
There is no division of the duties.

Then the statement in the public press was not correct, and the department is under the administration of the hon. gentleman the same as it was under the ex-Minister of Public Works. Is that correct 1

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think this is outside the question before the Chair.

I do not think it is, Mr. Chairman. We are discussing the items for the province of Quebec. The rumour went abroad that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had control over certain works in the province of Quebec in connection with harbours and rivers, and I think it is quite in order for us to inquire whether that is the case.
I think I gave the hon. gentleman a very definite answer.

These statements with respect to the division of the office were supposed to have emanated from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself. As he is here, we would like to hear from him as to whether there is any foundation for these reports in the papers. And would he tell us whether he made any such statements anywhere in the province of Quebec about the time he was elevated to the cabinet ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister said there was no division of the duties, and the hon. gentleman is bound to accept his statement.

I think a similar statement was made by the Prime Minister himself, and I am sure I read in the press that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries also had made that statement. It was remarked at the time that there was some little disappointment throughout the province of Quebec on account of him losing the cabinet position of Minister of Public Works, which had been held in that province for a great many years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) is out of order.
I beg pardon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, with all deference, I do not see how the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) are out of order.
What reference have they to the subject ?

They have this reference to the subject; we have the right to know whether or not particular items which the committee is asked to vote are to be expended under the direction of the hon. Minister of Public Works or under the direc-

tioii of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
That has been answered.
The information has been given.
I know it has been answered, but we are pointing out that other things have been said on the subject by the hon. gentleman which are somewhat inconsistent-
1 know the difference between a statute and a few loose remarks.

If the hon. Postmaster General desires to apply to the observations of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the term ' a few loose remarks ' I have no objection, although I would not be prepared to apply an expression of that kind to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am ready to give his remarks a little more weight than that. Every one knows, indeed, it has been generally stated in the province of Quebec, in the public press, and there is no repudiation toy the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries so far as I know, that lie announced to the people of that province that a considerable portion of that which previously was under the jurisdiction of the hon. Minister of Public Works is to be under his jurisdiction as Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It was announced during his election campaign- I saw it over and over again in the public press of the province of Quebec, and 1 have a perfect right to ask how it is that the hon. Minister of Public Works makes a statement now that is absolutely inconsistent with the statement made by his colleague in the province of Quebec at the time he was running his election. It is due to the committee, that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries should state his understanding of the situation in view of the observations which have been made by the hon. Minister of Public Works to-day, or that he should state to the committee that the announcement credited to him in the public press was credited to him improperly and without authority from himself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item be adopted ?
No, it shall not be adopted until we get more information upon this subject.

What is the information which the hon. gentleman desires ? I understand him to say that the committee have a right to know whether this item, which is now presented, is to be expended by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the hon. Minister of Public Works ? That is a perfectly proper Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
question, and it has been answered. There has been no division of the departments. If there is to be a division of either of these two departments legislation will be brought down for that purpose, and then, and not till then, will the House have a right to criticise such a proceeding.

Did the hon. Minister ofi Marine and Fisheries have the authority of the government to make the announcement which he did at that time that there was to be a change in the policy of this government ? That such an announcement was made by a member of the government in that province is beyond doubt. Did the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries have the right without authority from this government to make that announcement to the people of the province of Quebec ?

Whether he had or whether he had not may be properly the subject of a question put before the House after notice in the proper way, but I do not admit that the hon. gentleman has any right to level a question across the floor of the House and demand an answer categorically-yes or no. The policy of the government in this matter will be indicated by legislation proposed in this House, and then, and not till then, will the hon. gentleman have the right to criticise it.

Then, that means, if it means anything, that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries had no authority from the government to make the announcement which he did. I agree with the hon. Minister of Finance, that it would be proper that any policy of this government in regard to the matter should be first announced to this House when this House is in session. But that is not the case which we have before us. We have had the important announcement made by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries during his election campaign in the province of Quebec, we have had this House in session for more than six weeks, and we have not had one single word from the government about it. The hon. Minister of Finance takes the ground that the government want notice about a matter which was announced two months ago by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. We want to know if the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries had the sanction of his colleagues for this statement, or if he had not. It seems to me a very proper question for me to ask across the floor of this House, whether or not the hon. gentleman in making that announcement to the people of the province of Quebec had the authority or sanction of his colleagues.

The hon. gentleman has the right to ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries in proper

and regular form whether he made that announcement, but he has not the right to assume that such an announcement has been made, or to require an answer in +he manner in which he has brought the matter before the Committee.
I have made my statement in what I supposed to be a courteous way.
I am not questioning the courtesy of the hon. gentleman.

1 have stated two or three times that I, myself, have seen this announcement in the public press credited to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I have also said that I have seen no repudiation by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries of this statement so attributed to him. Then, I heard from the hon. Minister of Public Works something which I regard as somewhat inconsistent with this announcement so made. The hon. Minister of Finance takes refuge in this that he says the policy of the government should be announced to the House. I agree that it should be announced to the House, but, if the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries acted properly and with the sanction of his colleagues, why was not this policy announced to the House long ago ? This House has been in session for six weeks. Surely, the House, after the announcement which was made by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is entitled as a matter of courtesy, if for no other reason, to hear what the policy of the government is in regard to this matter. Surely the hon. Minister of Finance sees the position in which his colleague is placed. That was an announcement made to the people of the province of Quebec in an election in which the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries sought the suffrages of his constituents in that province, and whose confidence was somewhat shaken. It was publicly stated that there was some disappointment among the followers of the government there, that an important department like the Public Works Department had been allotted to a gentleman from another province. It was not only in the public press, but privately as well, that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries made these statements. Surely it is not asking too much to know at this stage, six weeks after the session has begun, and two or three months after the announcement was made, whether or not this is the policy of the government, or whether the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in making the statement he did make, acted entirely without consultation with his colleagues, and entirely without their sanction. I regard it as a very important thing whether or not the Department of Public Works is to be cut up in the way in which the hon.
Minister of Marine and Fisheries announced it is to he cut up. It is a matter that concerns very much the public interest of this country to know whether this announcement is true, and I do not think we are departing at all from our rights as an opposition in this House in asking that this information should be given to the people as to the policy of the government in regard to this question.

I was going to say that I think the proper time for giving this information was when the ministerial changes were announced to the House.
