Since it was not given then, it cannot be out of place for any member of this House to make an inquiry, especially as the two departments have been so intermixed, if we can believe what we have seen in the press. I have no doubt that the Minister of Marine (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) gave that information to his constituents so as to get their endorsation. Now, as to the item, the Minister of Public Works tells us that it is for erecting some kind of a shelter.
For the extension of buildings.
Then the item is improperly described, for it would read as if it were for extending a wharf and not a building.
My hon. friend is right. It does extend the wharf, but, it is also for the building of a freight shed on the wharf.

I know this place very well. The wharf is too low and when there is a strong wind the spray comes over the wharf and inconveniences the passenger trade at this place which is a summer resort. The wharf is to be made higher and wider and the shed is to be improved. Am I venturing too far in asking whether this item will be spent under the Department of Public Works.
It will.

There is no doubt whatever that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) stated during his election campaign that the Department of Public Works would be divided. I could never understand what portion of that department would be divided. Of course this is not the time to discuss the policy of the government on that point, but as having contributed to the best of my ability to organize the Department of Public Works as it is now, I would be very sorry indeed to see it divided. I suppose we will have the pleasure of hearing the policy of the government announced very soon.
If the Auditor General does his duty he will allow this money to be expended only for the purposes set forth i in this item.
This is for a small extension of the wharf which gives more space, and the criticism of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is right that the words in the estimates are somewhat misleading.
The reorganization of the department was mentioned in the speech from the Throne, and on that account I thought it perfectly right to mention the matter now.
I take no objection at all.

While it may not be a desirable time to discuss the question of policy, I do not see why the government should not be in a position to make some announcement to the House as to its policy on this matter, it now being six weeks after the opening of the session and two or three months after the announcement was made by the Minister of Marine (Hon. Mr. PrCfontaine) ; an announcement which in many parts of the country at least is regarded as largely affecting the public interest. I would like to know from the First Minister when he will make an announcement as to the policy of the government on this matter.
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden) agrees that this is not a convenient time to announce the policy of the government, but I have no objection to state that it will be announced at an early date.
That will mean Monday I suppose ?
Oh, no.
It has been announced in the speech from the Throne that this division would take place.

Oh, yes, it was announced in a far more important place than the speech from the Throne ; it was announced during the Maisonneuve election for a special purpose.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). And many more details were given during the Maisonneuve campaign than my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross) will find in the speech from the Throne. We are anxious to know whether the details given by the minister (Hon. Mr. Pr6fontaine) during his election campaign represent the policy which the government has decided on.
In justice to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prfifon-taine)-
Who has fled.

Who has gone out of the chamber, I should say that he appeared very willing to give us the information, but for some reason or other the hon. gentleman who at the time was leading the Mr. SPROULE.
House declined to allow him. We do not know why this was.
We do.
I suppose the Minister of Justice does know. Perhaps they were a little afraid of the discretion of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that he might say too much.
He has been doing that.

Perhaps this is why the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. PrCfontaine) made the announcement in Maisonneuve. The newspapers in Montreal at that time described him as a prospective candidate for the portfolio of Public Works and not of Marine and Fisheries, and he felt that his importance would vanish if he did not get some of the public works to administer. He was referred to in no very complimentary terms by the Montreal ' Witness,' that great Liberal exponent in the province of Quebec, which is widely read in Ontario and throughout the Dominion. I have not under my hand any of the statements that were made by the Montreal 'Witness,' but they are matters of public notoriety, and I must congratulate the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, on being so vigorous a fighter that he lias been able to break down all the opposition of the ' Witness' and bring himself to the front. When it was found that the hon. gentleman's nose was to come under the wire, so to speak, another opponent arose in the person of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, and perhaps that may be another reason why the hon. Minister of Agriculture is not here. It may be that he has gone away in order to cover up his disappointment and discomfiture at having to sit in the cabinet with the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It is well known that the Minister of Agriculture is one of the largest stock holders in the Montreal ' Herald ' company ; that is common report, and he has never denied it. It goes without saying that the Prime Minister must have a heavy task on his hands in reconciling these two warring elements in the cabinet. The Minister of Agriculture poses before the public as an exemplar of all that is good and proper, and yet through the col-ums of his own journal he assails the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the strongest terms. But the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to be congratulated on the fact that he prevailed on the Prime Minister to accept him despite all the violent attacks that had been made upon him by the journal owned and controlled to a great extent by the Minister of Agriculture. Reflections were made upon the hon. gentleman not only as a parliamentarian or as an old member of the House; but he was assailed by the Montreal ' Herald ' in terms so strong that I think he had fair ground for an action for libel against that journal. He was assailed while chief magistrate of the city of Mont-

real as having always acted for his own private interest instead of for the interest of the city. And this is such a wonderful cabinet, that its members can war against each other outside, and can placard each other in this way before the world, and yet be bound together in happy union by the cement of salary. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is a bonny fighter, and I congratulate him on having come to the front despite all these attacks. But he owes something to himself; he owes something first to his own self-respect, because he has made the statement publicly in the city of Montreal that while he was not to receive the Department of Public Works which had been assigned to the province of Quebec, I may say almost since confederation-

['I think we shall probably continue the supply for the first day. If we get through with other business on Monday, we will go on with the Public Works estimates, and if there is to be any change for Tuesday, the hon. gentleman will have an intimation of it on Monday.']

When you left the Chair, Mr. Chairman, I was making some remaks with reference to the statements made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) as to the division of the work of the Public Works Department. But as that hon. gentleman is not in his place, I do not propose to discuss the matter further. I may perhaps do so on some future occasion.
Newport breakwater-extension, $8,000.
This vote is to provide for the completion of a breakwater on the west side of the entrance of Newport river, and extending the cribwork 200 feet to a depth of 15 feet at low water.

This is a revote. Why was the work not gone on with ?
72i

They could not prepare the timber. A portion of the work was done in 1901. For the extension, it is proposed to call for tenders and let the work by contract.
Nicolet River-dredging, &c., $12,000.
This is to cover the expense of riprapping and repairing the jetty built at the mouth of the Nicolet river at Lake St. Peter. The dredging is to secure a depth of 8 feet at low water.
This is not all for dredging ?

If my hon. friend will notice, he will see that it is for ' dredging, &c.' The estimate of the engineer is $8,000 for dredging and $4,000 for riprapping and other work.
Pointe aux Esquimaux, wharf-headblock, $5,000.
Will the minister say what the department paid for this in the first place ? I see 1 Lavoie, Elie, interest due on purchase price of his wharf,' appears in the Auditor General's Report.
This work was built by the department in the first place at a cost of a little over $10,900.
Does this complete the work ?
This is to complete the extension of the work.

I might ask a general question, the answer to which may obviate the necessity of repeating the question on each vote. I understand the minister to say that in future the department will let these works by tender.

That is the clear intention on all works in which that can be done. I have mentioned, with regard to the last vote, that though in the past part of that work has been done by day's labour, we have changed the system and are letting it by contract.
Pointe St. Pierre-'breakwater, $22,000.
This work is now under contract.
What is the amount of the contract ?
It is $22,000. The estimated total cost of the breakwater is $24,000.

I notice that last year when there was an item up for this breakwater, the minister stated that the total cost would be $14,000, and that it was let by contract at that time for the sum of $14,000.

22a0
That must have been a mistake, because I find on reference to the papers of the department that the contract was let on the 4th of September, 1902, for the sum of $22,000.

It is reported in ' Hansard ' that the Minister of Public Works said, ' $14,000 is the estimate, and it is let by contract.' Would the minister state whether the engineer recommended the increased amount, or why the statement was made last year that $14,000 would complete the work, and now such a large increase is required.

I cannot account for the statement. It must either have been made under a misapprehension, or else misreported. Because the report of the engineers was that it would cost over $20,000, and the work could not have been under contract then, because it was only let last fall.

You spent on this work last year $2,000. Did you commence the expenditure before you let the contract ? I see that of the $10,000 voted last year you spent $2,000, and you have revoted the $8,000. That will make the whole work cost $24,000.

The estimate is that $2,000 will be spent before the 30th of June next, and we re vote $8,000 of last year's vote.
RiviSre aux Renards-breakwater, pier, $14,000.

This is for the purpose of extending the pier to a point on the east side of the harbour at the north of Fox river. It is now 300 feet long, and is to be extended to a length of 600 feet and to reach a depth of eighteen feet at low water. The total estimated cost of this work is $48,000.
Is it an old work or a new work ?
This extension is a new work.
Tenders are being called for now.
Some time ago this work was started by day labour and 300 feet of it was built. The intention is to extend that, and tenders have been asked for.
What county is this in ?
Gaspe. The whole work is to cost $48,000. The contract is not yet let for the balance of the work. But tenders have been advertised for.
We have not much information as to the necessity of the work.

I may tell my hon. friend that this is the only harbour of refuge on that coast. The county of GaspS is a very large county, with 250 miles of shore. Boats and schooners coming from the Labrador coast on the north shore, and from the Gulf of St. Lawrence, find there the only refuge on the Gaspe coast. It is the most important of all the works now being carried on on that coast.
What is the size of the place where this is built ?
The population of Fox river is about 1,000. There is considerable shipping there.
It is principally a place of refuge, I suppose ?

Yes.
RiviSre Batiscan-To continue dredging of channel at outlet of river, $5,000.
This is in Champlain county. It is to continue the navigable channel at the mouth of the river Batiscan to a depth of five feet at low water. This work is being done by contract.
Have the government no dredges down there of their own ?
Not at present.
What is the advantage of this work ?
I understand that large milling operations are carried on there.
The International Paper Company have an establishment there.
What mills have they there ?

Mills for pulp wood. The Price Bros, have very large limits on the Batiscan river. Formerly they had their mills up at a place called Ste. Genevieve, and they used to manufacture their logs into lumber at that point and then float the lumber down the river and load their ships' off the Batiscan river. But recently they have found it more convenient to bring their logs down to the entrance of the river and have abandoned their place at Ste. Genevieve. The result is that they now bring their vessels into the Batiscan river as far as possible in order to load near the mills.
Riviere Chateauguay-dredging, $5,000.
This is to c&ntinue the channel dredging commenced in 1898 at the mouth of the Chateauguay river.
What does this serve ?
This is to improve the general navigation of the Chateauguay river.

1 would like to know something of the advantage to be obtained by expending this money. I am not very familiar with the district although X know something of it. I do not know of anything that could warrant us in making such an expenditure.

I do not know that I am able to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) any statistics as to the amount of trade done there. The department has been doing the work for a great many years of improving the navigation of that river. There is a sandy bottom and the river bed fills up often. I am informed although I have no personal knowledge, that there is quite a little shipping.
Can the hon. minister give us any idea from his engineer what amount of money has been previously expended at this place ? It seems to be new to me.
I will be very pleased to have a statement made up.
We will let this item stand, until the information is obtained.

Stands.
Item allowed to stand.
Riviere du Loup-wharf, improvements and repairs, $3,500.
This is to cover the cost of building a new slip on the east side of the head lock of the Riviere du Loup pier.

What is the necessity of a new slip on the east side of the head lock of the Riviere du Loup pier ? I think the business of the House and particularly the consideration of items in regard to public works would be expedited, if, upon placing an item before the committee, the hon. Minister of Public Works would in the first instance give us some reasonable amount of information to avoid the necessity of asking so many questions. I would suggest that he might always tell the committee when the particular work is to be undertaken, where it is, why it is necessary\_when and why the work has been commenced, what are the objects and advantages of the work, when it is to be finished, whether it is being done by contract, the amount already expended, the total estimate of what it will cost and the population to be benefited. Information of this kind, I think, if given, would expedite the work of the committee.

I think the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition is quite a proper one. Even if I have information on hand it would perhaps not be given so fully in regard to a place like this as almost every hon. member is familiar with the locality and perhaps in regard to these main estimates the great
majority of the items deal with the continuation of works that the House was committed to not only last session but during previous sessions.
Of course, that may be true, but we cannot be expected to carry these facts in our minds in the same way as the hon. minister does.

I quite agree with the suggestion which the hon. gentleman has made. In regard to the Riviere du Loup wharf I think we are all familiar with the locality. I suppose that it is not necessary for me to take up the time of the House in referring to the importance of Rivi6re dfl Loup as a shipping point. The chief engineer informs me that the fixed slip there has been of no service on account of the movable tides and it is proposed to build a new movable slip.
River *St. Francis-ice piers at Richmond
What is this for ?

This is a vote of $11,000 to provide for the completion of the projected four ice breaking piers to be built under contract in the River St. Francis a short distance below Richmond, the object being to prevent as far as practicable, the recurrence of the destruction that is caused by ice jams in the narrows between the town and the Grand Trunk railway bridge, about a mile and a quarter below. This work is under contract. The amount of the contract is $11,317 and the total estimate of the cost of- the work is $12,000.

When we are expending $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 in this country perhaps it is inopportune for me to criticise the expenditure of $11,000 as this item has reference to my own immediate section of the country. I suppose that the people in the eastern townships should congratulate themselves that the government have recognized that St. Francis river is worthy of their attention. There is no shipping on the St. Francis river. It is not navigable. This is entirely beyond what I think even the mqpt elastic sort of kindly dispensation on the' part of the government would consider within the realm of financial assistance from the central government. I am surprised and it only indicates, Mr. Chairman, that we are running extremely wild in the direction of offering assistance when we look at this item. It is quite true that the raising of the water in that section, as in many small rivers in all parts of Canada, occasionally takes away a bridge here and there which the municipalities have more or less borne the burden of replacing. Such was the case in Richmond, such was the case just above Richmond at the town of Brampton where they lost a bridge. We have had such an experience in the com-

munity where I live but we hare never thought of coming to the Dominion government to construct piers to guard these peculiar flows of water and ice in extraordinary seasons in these small streams and I must say that if this item is voted it is a precedent without limit, because, we could not consider any loss by water anywhere on any stream in the Dominion of Canada that would not result in a demand on this parliament to vote assistance for preventing the recurrence of such mishaps. I am perfectly astonished at seeing this item here and I cannot conceive that the hon. minister has been put in possession of all the facts of the case. He has been asked to do what is purely a municipal work and if* not a municipal work, if it is to receive the slightest aid from any other direction than the municipality, it must come from a provincial source. I can scarcely believe that the Dom-ion government could consider this work for the general benefit of Canada. I think the minister must have been misled. I do not believe that if he knew the circumstances he would ever have established such a precedent because it leaves him open to all sorts of demands whenever trouble arises on any small unnavigable stream in Canada. If we were in the local legislature and this imposed an extraordinary burden upon the municipality, there might be some ground for considering it under unusual circumstances but to come to the Dominion parliament to ask money for such a purpose is really absurd. It is a dangerous precedent and should not be sanctioned by this House.

The hon. gentleman must remember that parliament committed itself to this expenditure last session. There may be a good deal in the statement that he has made, but I assume that a full explanation was given a year ago as to why the money was appropriated.
Has the work been done ?
The work is under contract and parliament is pledged to carry it out. I must he frank in saying that I have not gone into the details as to why parliament uHdertook this work in the first place.

There does not seem to be any way of condemning the department for an expenditure like this. Although the minister is a new Minister of Public Works he is not a new member of the cabinet and he has to share responsibility with his colleagues for this kind of thing. I am surprised that the present minister, or the exminister, or no minister at all should have sanctioned a thing like this. In fact an ordinary member of parliament drawing the magnificent salary of $1,500 a year would have been more careful before entering into such an expenditure. If this item should Mr. POPE.
pass every municipality in the country would be justified in presenting bills to the Dominion government in connection with the improvement of small rivers. That is a fact, Mr. Minister, and whether it is you or your predecessor who is responsible, or both of you combined, you are pledged for all time to bear burdens which ought to be borne by the municipalities interested. I wish to enter my protest against this. I suppose it is not necessary that I should move that this item be struck out in order to emphasize my protest, because 'Hansard' is here and it will be known in future that I have protested. I here and now enter my protest. I am pleased and displeased at this. I am pleased because I know the locality and can speak with knowledge when I protest against this vote, and I am displeased that such an expenditure of Dominion public money should be made in that district upon works that are absolutely and purely municipal.

This is a dangerous precedent and we cannot too soon protest against it. You might as well go down to the Rideau river here and help the municipality to build the bridge which has been swept away two or three times. As the hon. member (Mr. Pope) has well said, this item is for a purely municipal work and if the burden is too heavy for the municipality then the provincial government and not the Dominion government should come to its assistance. It turns out now that this river is not navigable, and that this bridge is just for the convenience of the travelling public.
My hon. friend (Mr. Pope) is mistaken ; this is a navigable river.
No.
No part of it ?
No navigation on it whatever, except perhaps at the mouth.

There are many navigable rivers on which they have no boats running, but I am told this river is navigable. As I have explained, this vote is not for a bridge but for an ice breaking pier. The engineer of the department informs me that representations were made that a great deal of valuable land was flooded at times. Of course, as a member of the government I have to assume responsibility, but we are all responsible to a certain extent for commencing this work because it has been approved by parliament.

As the minister knows, I have never had the extreme honour of being a member of a government, and I would like to know how it could come about that such an expenditure as this would be considered by a Dominion cabinet sitting to consider

national affairs. What have they to do with municipal matters ? Who petitioned for this expenditure ?

The information in the department is that there was a petition from the town council of Richmond to the Minister of Public Works and he no doubt recommended it to council and council was responsible for recommending it to parliament.
I suppose some official was sent to report as to whether or not this work was of national importance.
The chief engineer informs me that the only report asked for was as to the effect this work would have on the flooding of these lands, and the cost of the work.
Am I to understand that the construction of these piers is going to stop the flooding of that river ?
That is the opinion of the engineers.

I can understand the petition of the municipality, and I am very sorry I had not known before of the parental character of this government, because I know of many instances in which they could have had petitions for local works from municipalities in the part of the country where I live. It would relieve us of a great deal of taxation. We have laboured under the misapprehension that the moneys of Canada were for the special work of Canada ; but we are now face to face with the fact that this government is not only Dominion in its character, but that it has even gone beyond the bounds of the provinces, and has become a municipal organization. That is a kindly disposition and an encouragement to men to live in Canada. We can say to the municipalities that they need not be too careful in their expenditures, for in adversity they can come to the Dominion government for relief. I am pleased to get this much information, for we live in a mountainous region where the currents run swiftly and the waters rise rapidly, and where we have to contend every year more or less with floods, and I shall be pleased in the future to recommend to the municipalities in my section that they need not further consider extraordinary expenditures, for they have a right to appeal to this government. Every river in our section is as navigable as this River St. Francis. In August or September you could not take a boat up the St. Francis river unless it had a flat bottom. It is not a navigable river at all. I do not believe the members of the council ever considered this item, and I am astonished that the Dominion parliament should be spending its time voting money for municipal purposes. It is an absolute and positive disgrace.
Riviere St. Maurice, between Grandes Piles and La Tuque, $8,000.
This is for operating the government dredge on this river.
Last year, out of a vote of $8,000, something like $5,955 was expended. Do you propose to perform the same work again this year ?

It is estimated that 3,000,000 logs will be floated down that river this season. This dredging is to remove the sand bars which have formed, and which would otherwise prevent the logs being floated down.

How many yards is that dredge.supposed to take out in a day, and -what is the estimated cost of operating it ? That will give us an approximate idea of the difference between dredging by government and dredging by contract.

I am told by the engineer that it will take out about 300 yards a day, and its maintenance will cost about $25 per day.
Riviere St. Maurice-dredging eastern channel,

This is to provide for further dredging in the eastern channel.
Rivi6re Touladie-improvement of, $2,000.
What kind of work is the department carrying out there ?
This is to make provision for the improvement of the navigation of the upper reaches of the river by the construction of a flat dam.
How much of the work was done last year ?
None was done last year. There was a survey.
How much will this work cost ?
The chief engineer says he has not had time yet to estimate the total cost of this work.
I think it. will cost a pretty large amount of money. It is an important river in a section of the country where considerable settlement is going in.
Is there any water in the river ?
I do not know the depth of the water. I have not the report under my hand, and I do not think the survey was in when I left office.

There are petitions from the settlers for this improvement. Unless it is found that this money can be expended to the advantage of the district, in accordance with the

petitions of the settlers, and without incurring too heavy an expenditure, I should not feel bound to expend the money at all. If, on the other hand, the vote of $2,000, which was given last year, will give navigation for the benefit of the district, there should be no objection to making these improvements.
What is the object of making them ?
To overcome the rapids that exist.

Is the stream navigable?
. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Yes, for small boats.

Settlers are going into that district. I am stating what is represented by the petitions which are in the department. This is in the riding of Ternis-couata, about fifty or sixty miles from Fraserville. It is a very fertile district, and there are important groups of settlers in it. They made representations that it would be useful to them to have the river made clear for navigation. When the item was put in the estimates last year, we had no information, but we ordered a survey and the report should be in now. We were told that the river could be improved a distance of forty or fifty miles by wing dams, removal of rocks and so on.
The difficulty seems to be that the hon. minister has not the slightest idea what the work will cost when completed.

That seemed to be the position when the vote was taken. I have said that if an expenditure of $2,000 will remove the obstructions and make this stream navigable even one-half the distance represented, instead of forty or fifty miles, it would be a very desirable expenditure. On the con-tray, if the report shows that this expenditure will not be of any service and that it would cost a large sum to make this stream navigable, I would feel pledged not to spend the money.

I would infer from the discussion that it is apparently the policy of the government to improve small streams running through any section of the coun-. try, whether these streams be navigable or not, in order to accommodate settlers and enable saw mill owners to run their logs down them. If that be the case, we have several small streams in the province of Ontario, in which some of my constituents are very much interested, and where the expenditure of public money for the purpose of improving them would be very desirable. If it is the policy of the government to do this work in the province of Quebc, we would like to have it turn its attention to the province of Ontario. I have been lum-

bering on a stream for thirty-one years and have built my own dams in order to run my logs down that stream. The provincial government of Ontario sold the lands there, thirty-one years ago, at ten times the price which they receive for the best agricultural lands in that section. They have received the money for those lands, and a stream runs through them, down which I have been floating my logs. It is not a navigable stream but may be called navigable for the purpose of running logs. It is certainly not navigable for boats or steamers for the transportation of agricultural products. A requisition has been made by the residents in two of the municipalities to the provincial government for a grant to enable them to remove the obstructions from the stream and to enable the farmers to drain their land. Requisitions and petitions have been presented from the municipalities and the councils of the different municipalities, but apparently we have not approached the proper authorities. I have received notice to attend a meeting next Wednesday to interview the premier of Ontario, and I expect the corporations of two or three municipalities to be present. If we do not succeed in bringing sufficient influence to bear on the provincial premier to make us a liberal grant, I shall certainly advise the municipality to apply to this government.

There is another side to the story. On several occasions I was induced to promise large improvements on rivers like the one under discussion. It was represented to me that the improvement would help settlement in these districts. We are spending a large amount in bringing out foreign immigration, especially to the west. The older provinces do not get much to help them in their immigration policy. It was represented to me in this case that by improving the river, we would give means of communication to a number of new settlers. It is a part of the country which is now being settled step by step. Is the federal government justified in carrying out improvements on rivers in such cases ? I believe we are.
It is very doubtful.
I know it is a debate-able question, but we are spending a large amount of money in order to send the settlers to the west
Canada.

The Touladie is also Canada. Suppose we spend a few thousand dollars and the result will be to have 500 settlers there, that will be money well invested. Of course, I am speaking now in a general way. The question is worth debating and it is a very interesting one. I fully grant that on many occasions we are led into making expenditures, that, perhaps we should not make. But I call the atten-

tion of the Committee to this other side of the question. When the government, by improving the rivers or building wharfs around the lakes, as in the case of lake St. John, can help in settling the country, I think the expenditure is justified.
St. Alexis Baie des Ha Ha-pier, $4,000.
Is that under contract?
The work, so far has been done by day labour. It will require $8,000 according to the estimates of the engineer to complete the work. The amount expended is $20,000.
That has been spent by day labour ? Is that to be continued ?
I think it will be better, if practicable, that we should let that by contract.
What is the work ?

The work when completed will cost $22,000, of which $20,000 has already been spent, the work being done by day labour. If, on looking into conditions, I find that it is practicable, I would prefer to let the balance by contract.
How much was done last year ?
Work to the value of $3,994.
The Auditor General's Report says that over $4,000 was spent.
That is the amount spent last fiscal year. I was giving what was spent up to the 31st of December last, which was $3,994.
What is the work ?
Building a wharf.

And does the hon. minister mean to say the department has been five or six years; in building a wharf at a cost of $32,000 ? It seems to me that if the community for whose use this wharf is intended did not want it any sooner than that, they did not need it at all.

The attempt is sometimes made to justify such an expenditure as this by saying that settlers are coming into the district. Are these settlers coming in from another country or only from another part of the province ?

So far as that part of the province is concerned, I am glad to say that most of the settlers are coming from the United States-some of them, of course, from other parts of this country. But there is a good stream of immigration from the United States going in just now. The Quebec Colonization Company is doing a very good work indeed. I quite grant that it may
seem surprising that works of this kind have been started by day labour. Let me say that, right or wrong, I have been induced, on several occasions, to carry out such work by day labour, to help the settlement of some parts of the country. I am sure that when you can find a good local engineer and foreman, you can carry on works as well by day labour as by contract. Of course, my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has made up his mind to have such works carried on by contract. I do not blame him, for that will relieve him of a great deal of trouble.

I agree with the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that, under some circumstances, you can get good value by day labour. But, where a work covers a period of five or six years, the cost of overseeing, etc., is so high that I think it is better to let the work by contract.
I can not understand what they were doing if they occupied five or six years in spending $32,000.

I am sure that if the hon. minister looks into it, he will see that it was not intended to take so much time as that I fully expected it would be completed within two years. It takes one year to prepare and bring out the material-
And another year to put it together. That is enough, if the work is necessary, and if it is not, it would be better to abandon it.

It seems to me that if the timbers were got out six or seven years before being used, they would be rotten, and it would be necessary to get out another set.
St. Andre de Kamouraska-to complete repairs to earth approach to pier, &c., $750.
This is to complete the repairs. The earth embankment or approach to the wharf was commenced in 1892-3. These repairs were begun last year.
This is an old wharf.

Yes, but these repairs were begun last year.
St. Francois-pier on south shore of Isle of Orleans, $0,000.
This is to provide for building a government pier to be constructed under contract on the south shore of the Island of Orleans.
When was this begun, and how much is it to cost ?

The contract was made on the 7th February last, for $11,800. The total estimated cost is $13,000.

St. Irgnee wharf-construction of headbloek and repairs, $3,600.

This work is under contract, made on the 24th January last for $10,399. The total estimated cost of the work is $12,900.
St. Jerome (Lake St. John) wharf, $2,000.
This is to complete the extension of the wharf under construction. The object is to reach a depth of six feet at the lowest water of Lake St. John.
When was the wharf on Lake St. John built ?

In 1889. There is three feet of water, and the idea is to have six feet of water for a distance of 170 feet. This has all been done by day labour.
Sorel, deep water wharf, $47,000.
What is this, Mr. Minister ?

This is to complete the payment on the contract for building this work at Sorel. The contract was $255,632.43. The contractors are Poupore & Malone. The estimated cost of the work is $273,500. This $47,000 will complete the payment of the present contract.

This is a very large amount of money for a place like Sorel, and I think it is worthy of the consideration of this Committee. Of course, I am willing to admit that perhaps I come in a little late in criticising this item, since this expenditure has been going on for a year or two. I know the town of Sorel somewhat.
The city of Sorel.

I am much surprised to find we are spending this amount of money there. I would like that item to stand over until we can have the fullest possible information with regard to it, if the minister has no objection. Some of the information we require might take a little time to get. I don't think we should be called upon to pass this item without knowing ail the conditions and circumstances connected with so large an expenditure of money.
What conditions and circumstances does my hon. friend refer to ?
You are hard on the poor fishermen.

No, I am not, in fact my heart goes forth unto the fishermen, and to my hon. friend who has to represent them. I sympathize with him also, because it is fortunate for him that his county is 250 miles long, or we would have had it piered all round. In fact I think he has no peer in this House in getting piers. But, Sir, this town of Sorel is an old settled place in which I would really like to know the amount of business that is being done, the tonnage, and all those particulars, before I think we can proceed with this matter.

I understand an explanation was given at the time this large vote was made. Perhaps the tonnage at the present time is not very large, but a new railroad is being built, and then the building of this wharf to get a deep draught will create a large trade.
What railroad is this ?
The United Counties railway.
Has it been running all this winter ?
I do not think it is running daily.
No, nor weekly either.

I am responsible for the presence of this item in the estimates. My colleagues are just as much responsible as I am, because it is not a departmental question by any means. The question was considered with every possible care. It was represented to the government that there would be a large trade for that town if that deep water wharf was built. Dr. Seward Webb and his associates were often in the country in those days. They had large schemes.
And private cars.

They are not the only ones who have private cars. However, it

was represented that it would be a good thing if they had deep water communication. The question was discussed last year, and I stated the facts which I am stating now. Unfortunately, all these promises have not materialized. The South Shore railway is running occasionally.
Hear, hear.

The United Counties railway has been closed. I do not know what the future of these two railways will be. But there were strong influences behind the project, and the government thought it was a reasonable thing to do. The Prime Minister from his seat last year defended the item from the standpoint of the general development of trade. The work is under contract. I hope that things will be better in the future than they have been during the last year or so, because these two roads are in a bad shape indeed, to the great detriment of the people in that part of the country.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we do not seem to elicit-well, not tremendous applause from the ministers who are representing this department at the present time. I have listened to the minister who draws the salary and I have also listened to the minister who did draw the salary, and when I combine the voices of both of them I do not see that cheerful prospect for the future of a great trade for the great town of Sorel.
Sorel is a city.

I apologize-the great city of Sorel, and the great United Counties railroad that runs now and again from one point to another when it has a carload of stuff to take. Such items as these, I suppose, are legacies which have come down to the present hon. minister. I feel sorry for him. I feel sorry for the hon. ex-minister, because I do not think that the hon. ex-minister, or the present minister, is responsible. I think we will have to go to the government themselves and I think we will have to proceed further to the right hon. Prime Minister.
That is the man.

And I think we will have to proceed to the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) of St. Hyacinthe in which place there is a bank. I wonder where that hon. minister is. There is a bank at St. Hyacinthe that is seriously involved in this railway. They have put a good deal of the money of this bank into this railway, that is the railway that does not run with any time table, that does not run anywhere at any particular time and that has never been known to get anywhere at any time you wanted to get there. In the great city of Sorel we are spending $200,000 to build a wharf to provide for the traffic to be expected from the railway that never runs anywhere at any particular time. I think
this committee on this occasion should feel sad. I do. I think it is really a committee of mourning.
It was yesterday.

It is to-day. It is said too that in order to save the bank and in order to save a member of the government, the government should feel that they are warranted in spending $200,000 upon a city that cannot get its railway to run once a week. That railway has been shut up pretty nearly all winter. I do not know whether it is open yet or not. I do not believe that hon. members are aware of the conditions, or the small amount of tonnage handled. I am anxious to get that information. The hon. minister has not given it to me. If he has listened to the hon. gentleman who preceded me I think he ought to see that we should have this tonnage. I think we ought to get all the information in regard to this matter, and of course, if this committee has to swallow the pill, if it is necessary, in order that the right hon. Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue and other members of the government should be happy to vote this money, if these bon. gentlemen will confess that there is no business for this wharf, that there is no business to maintain the railway, that it is not a legitimate expenditure, but that it is to save their credit, I suppose this committee will accept it, but this committee cannot accept it as a business proposition. No. we must have the information. If the hon. Minister of Public Works asks us to accept of this expenditure on a business basis, on the ground that there is sufficient trade to warrant the construction of the wharf and that the roads that run from that wharf to the centres of the world carry a trade which warrants us in the construction of the work, I say that I cannot accept such a justification for the expenditure and I ask for the information as I have a right to ask for it. But, if the hon. minister says that we are doing this out of the kindness of our hearts in order to save some of our colleagues, or save some of our banks, we will have to take into consideration that view of the question. I must either consider it from the business point of view, or I must believe that these hon. gentlemen have some other motive than a business motive in proceeding with that work.

I am afraid I have not much more information to give the hon. gentleman than that which I have already given him. The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) recommended this work. My hon. friend (Mr. Pope) asked me for information in regard to the trade connected with this wharf. Up to the present I am sorry to say that it has not grown as fast as the ex-Minister of Public Works expected in connection with the building of this road

and other enterprises in that locality. The people may have been disappointed in the expectations which they formed at the time. When parliament committed itself to this expenditure three years ago, at whicll time the cost was known, and especially last session when $170,000 was voted to carry on the work, my hon. friends would have perhaps been more timely than they are now. I hope the picture is not quite so dark as be has painted it. While this has been a somewhat expensive work, this is an important district and there is a good deal of trade still to be done. The vote now under consideration, $47,000, is to complete the payments for work that was done some years ago under contract.

In so far as my not making serious objection last year to this work is concerned, I have the same plea to make as the hon. gentleman offered. I was not criticising last year. He avoids responsibility for that vote last year and for the organization of the work by saying that he was not the minister then.
No, I say that I assumed my responsibility with the hon. gentleman and with other hon. gentlemen in regard to this work.

The hon. Minister of Public Works charges the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) with the inauguration of this work. I differ from the hon. gentleman. The ex-Minister of Public Works was away at the time this money was first granted for this work. There was $25,000 granted for it during the absence of the ex-Minister of Public Works. He is not responsible for it any more than the present hon. Minister of Public Works is responsible, but the gentleman who really assumed the responsibility of making this an ocean port, was the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Last session he said that they proposed what was entirely a new work in 1899 or 1900 when they voted $25,000 for this work, and that they had surveys and estimates showing that it would cost to complete the work, something like $175,000 in order to make this an ocean port. That was the statement made by the'right lion. Prime Minister. Therefore, that being true, it would appear that the government as a whole undertook this work of making an ocean port at this place.

I have no intention of disclaiming the responsibility that is incumbent upon me. I am responsible for every item of expenditure that appears in the estimates of last year. I am perfectly prepared to take my share of it, but I think the hon. Minister of Public Works might have avoided saying that I inaugurated that work. I am responsible just the same as my former colleagues are. If there is any blame I will stand the blame manfully, but I have no more personal responsibility than the hon.
gentleman has. I know he did not mean to put it in that way.
I did not say so. I distinctly on several occasions assumed responsibility for the work. It is not right to say that I said so, because I neither insinuated it nor stated it.

I am responsible for that work, but the question was considered by the government as a whole. My colleagues who discussed the situation with mo will remember that the whole thing was carefully considered. I am responsible just as much as any other member of the government. We expected that things would turn out better than they have done. Strong representations were made to us and we yielded to these. Perhaps I was not here when the first amount was placed on the estimates, but that fact does not relieve me in any way. I am fully responsible and I do not disclaim that responsibility, but I do not want to be singled out as the one person responsible any more than any other member of the administration.

I have no reason to doubt what the hon. gentleman says, although I was not a member of the government at that time. A full explanation was given to the House as to what the cost of the work would be. If that work had been undertaken without giving the information to the House it would have been a different matter.

The responsibility is of course with the government. It is not with an individual member of the cabinet even as at present constituted, and much less is the responsibility with the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hori. Mr. Tarte), who has ceased to be a member of the cabinet. I would suggest to the hon. Minister of Public Works that as the Minister of Finance wants to put through three items which are rather urgent, we might let this vote stand for the present.

I have no objection at all, but as we have spent several sittings on this one resolution,
I would like as a compromise suggestion to put the remaining items through and let this one stand with another which already stands, on the understanding that they can be discussed if necessary.

Let us see what the other items are.
Three Rivers harbour-additional deep water wharfs, $100,000.

This vote of $100,000 is to make provision for carrying on during the fiscal year 1903-4 the works let by contract with a view of affording the additional deep water wharf accommodation called for by the Three Rivers Harbour Commission. This wharf

gives accommodation for handling coal, sulphur, and other bulky materials which are brought in for the use of railways and manufacturing establishments in the city and surrounding country. The amount of the contract was $280,500, and the contingencies will make the estimated total cost about $300,000.
How much of that work has been carried out ?

I find that very little of this work has been done, and not much has been paid on account. The contract was let on the 10th of June, 1902. The engineer of the department informs me that the contractors were not able to procure the timber and materials in time to get much work done last year.
When does the hon. minister expect that the work will be completed ? Is there any hope that the contractors will now go on with the work with some vigour ?
The contract provides that the work is to be completed on the 10th of June, 1904, and the chief engineer informs me that they have started now. I have no personal knowledge about it.
Who is the engineer in charge ?
Mr Lefebvre is the local engineer in charge of the work.
The minister says that this wharf will be used for importing coal and sulphur. What kind of industry do they intend to start there ?

There is more than that in it. Twenty-one miles north of Three Rivers is situated the manufacturing centre of Shawenegan Falls. There is the Belgo-Canadian Pulp Company, which manufactures pulp and paper ; and the carbide works, manufacturing aluminium and carbide of calcium. Eight miles further north, and twenty-nine miles from Three Rivers, is the Laurentide Pulp Company. To show you the increase of traffic in this locality, I may say that in 1898-9 there were taken down the river one and a half million pieces of timber, and in 1901-2 there were 3,272,261 pieces of timber which were manufactured in these localities. The trade is not all done through Three Rivers now because we have not the dock facilities, but it will be when the dock is built. As I have said before in this House, I do not think that money could be better expended, because I do not believe there is a more ideal spot in the whole Dominion of Canada for a national harbour than is Three Rivers. We have all these industries north of the town that I have mentioned, and we have also important industries in the city of Three Rivers. All these manufactured products,
and all the deals made from these logs are shipped across the ocean, and we have also the raw materials :	Brimstone, coal, clay
for the manufacture of aluminum, coming through Three Rivers. In past years we have not been able to take care of more than 20 per cent of the traffic which is within twenty-one miles of this deep water dock, because we did not have wharf facilities. This work will give us 2,020 feet additional of new dock. It will help transportation in the way, that now you have to haul from or to Quebec, and the only railway that goes through Shawenegan and Grand'M&re is the Great Northern, and they have the worst piece of track between Shawenegan and Grand'Mgre and Quebec that there is. When we are able to use this dock it will shorten the haul to twenty-one miles in lieu of a hundred miles. I may say also that when these docks are completed they will not be even then ample to accommodate all the traffic that is necessary for the country within a radius of twenty miles from Three Rivers.
I congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) on having something to ship from this wharf.
Thank you.

It is refreshing to know that we are expending money where there is trade to be done. There is no desire on this side of the House to object to any expenditure where there is justification for it, but what we do object to is making large expenditures in places where there is no trade and no necessity for expenditure.
Last year we loaded ninety-six ocean steamers at Three Rivers.

Montreal, Three Rivers, and Quebec should be equipped without delay.
Valleyfield-dredging, $4,000.
This is for keeping open the channel in Valleyfield bay. There has been some $15,000 spent there, and I am informed by the engineer that this will complete the work.
There is some dredging going on by the dredge ' St. Pierre ' which is paid $7 an hour. This Valleyfield dredge gets $8 an hour. What is the cause of the difference ?
The chief engineer informs me that this dredge has been improved, and has reached the standard of dredges that get $8 an hour.
What is the name of the dredge used in Valleyfield ?
There is no name that we have in the department. It is a dredge owned by the Canadian Construction Company of Montreal.

Before the Committee rises, perhaps X may be allowed to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he has read in ' Le Soleil ' of Quebec a despatch from Ottawa to the effect that the contract for the Quebec harbour works had been awarded to a gentleman named Dussault. As no new tenders have been asked, I was very much surprised to read the telegram.

I do not know why my hon. friend should be surprised. This work was advertised several weeks ago, and, as Dussault & Lemieux were the lowest tenderers, I have no doubt they were notified by the department that their tender would be accepted.
What work is that ? Is it the same -work that was advertised last year ?
Part of the same work-the same location. It is an extension of the wharf for about 500 feet.
But not the same plans.

I understand not the same plans.
Immigration-further amount required, $100,-
000.

In this sheet of supplementary estimates, which perhaps is not in the possession of all the members, though it was distributed some days ago, there are three items, and, if the Committee will permit me, I will speak of them all together. The items are :	Further amount required for immigration, $100,000 ; further amount required for services of North-west Mounted Police in the Yukon Territory, $150,000; and miscellaneous expenses in connection with the Alaska boundary tribunal, $50,000. After consultation with the hon. leader of the opposition, I am asking the Committee to agree to vote to-night the items for immigration and the Alaska boundary tribunal, with the understanding that both these matters will be open to discussion on other items which are still to come before the House. If the Prime Minister were in his seat, I would ask also that the item of $150,000 for the North-west Mounted Police be voted ; but that may stand until he is present. The items for immigration and for the Alaska boundary tribunal are urgent. That for immigration is required in consequence of the very large amount of work being done this season, the evidence of which we have in the great influx of people into the North-west Territories. For the expenses of the Alaska boundary tribunal $10,000 was taken by Governor General's warrant to start the proceedings, but that will only go a short distance, as there are heavy expenses connected with the employment of counsel and other matters in the

preparation of the case. I should be very glad if the Committee will vote these two items to-night with the understanding that at a later stage the whole matter will come up for discussion under other items.
Mi-. SPROULE. With regard to immigration, I think it is not indicative of very good business management that the government come down and ask for such a large item to close the financial year, in view of the fact that we gave them last year $445,000 or $450,000, which was the largest vote for immigration in a great many years. We were assured that there would be a great influx of immigrants this year, but you would think those who had the business in charge would be able to make a closer estimate than one which leaves them one dollar out in every four. It is not evidence that they are men of great business foresight or judgment. With regard to the class of immigrants which are coming in, while it is pleasing to note that the great mass of them are of the most desirable class, it is a fact that cannot be overlooked that there are a great many coming in Who are not the most desirable people.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the next government business to be taken up, whether on Monday or Tuesday ?

I think we shall probably continue the supply for the first day. If we get through with other business on Monday, we will go on with the Public Works estimates, and if there is to be any change for Tuesday, the hon. gentleman will have an intimation of it on Monday.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.15 p.m.
